finding.claim: Default ScpClient path quoting (RemotePathDoubleQuoteTransformation) escapes only double quotes, so attacker-influenced remote paths containing $(...), backticks, or a trailing backslash inject commands into the remote shell executed by 'scp -f'.
finding.source: Remote path string passed by the application to ScpClient.Download (e.g. a user-supplied or externally listed file name)
finding.sink: SendExecRequest("scp -f " + Transform(filename)) at ScpClient.cs:578; same pattern at :498, :538, :367, :410, :459

trace.note: filename is transformed and concatenated into the exec command
Transform wraps path in double quotes
Only '"' is escaped with a backslash; '$', backtick and '\' are not escaped
Class docs warn that unsuitable transformations can allow command execution

finding.guards_checked: Default transform is DoubleQuote, not the safe RemotePathShellQuoteTransformation; legacy parameterless constructors are [Obsolete] (ScpClient.cs:61-64); docs warn at ScpClient.cs:40-41. Hazard is documented but the default stays injectable. Impact requires the app to pass untrusted paths.

finding.claim: Host key verification fails open: with no HostKeyReceived subscriber CanTrustHostKey returns true, and HostKeyEventArgs defaults CanTrust to true, so any server host key is accepted.
finding.source: Network attacker (MITM) presenting its own host key with a valid signature over the exchange hash
finding.sink: Trust decision in ValidateExchangeHash: keyAlgorithm.VerifySignature(...) && CanTrustHostKey(keyAlgorithm) at KeyExchange.cs:493

trace.note: Signature verified against the host key the server presented, then CanTrustHostKey called
If HostKeyReceived has no handlers, the method falls through
Returns true when there is no handler
Constructor sets CanTrust = true, so a handler that does not explicitly set CanTrust=false accepts the key

finding.guards_checked: Signature check at KeyExchange.cs:493 only proves possession of the presented key, not its identity. No pinning or known_hosts logic exists in the library. Fail-open default may be deliberate but is security-relevant for authentication.

finding.claim: Host certificate verification does not check certificate type (host vs user) or principals (hostnames), and trusts whatever CA key is embedded in the certificate.
finding.source: Server-supplied host certificate; attacker is an insider holding a valid user certificate signed by a CA the app trusts, with network position

trace.note: Session signature checked against the certificate's public key
Signature checked against CA key taken from the certificate itself; no pinning
CertificateType enum exists (user/host) but is never compared in the host path
Principals documented as hostnames for host certificates, never matched to the connected host

finding.guards_checked: Session signature, validity period, CA signature checked. Certificate type and principal not checked. Application-side CA fingerprint pinning via HostKeyReceived is the only trust anchor. Severity low to medium, conditional on the CA also issuing user certificates.
